utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Therefore, I take it, Mr. Stojanovic, that you're ready to call your next witness, which is Mr. Kovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be Professor Milos Kovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated, Mr. Kovic. Mr. Kovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic who is now standing. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to speak slowly. We've already agreed to speak slowly, haven't we? Please give us your exact name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Milos Kovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you briefly tell us about your professional and academic career and your education.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: I teach at the University of Belgrade. I'm a lecturer of the faculty of philosophy. I teach history of the new age. I got my masters degree and my doctorate at that same university. I studied abroad as well. I attended various conferences. I also published several dozen professional papers, monographs, and other professional works. That is what I have to say for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the first time that you appear as an expert witness before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: I see that. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't hold it against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 65 ter 1D05903 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You will see before you on the screen the document that I've called up. That is your CV. And I would just like to ask you briefly: Are there any changes to the CV that you attached to your report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: I've published a few new books in the meantime that are relevant. For example, one about Gavrilo Princip who assassinated Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, this is a compilation of documents about him; and another paper that has to do with the attitude of the great powers towards Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of the Great Eastern Crisis. So these are the publications that I would like to add at this point in time. There were some others that are perhaps of no relevance for these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the CV of Milos Kovic, our expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do that just a question. Mr. Kovic, you said you studied abroad. Where did you study abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the University of Oxford, I underwent some advanced training there. You have it here in my CV. In 2004, 2005, I was working on my doctorate and I was a visiting doctoral student at the University of Oxford. You can see it in my CV here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D5903 will be Exhibit D1367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can the number be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do learn that there is no B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, 1D -- it's 65 ter 1D05903.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let me just -- no. Is that a different number from the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the same number. There's no B/C/S version uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think we can live with it in view of the character of the document and the impact on the Defence. But on -- Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just if we could confirm that the witness understands the English language because otherwise it would be a little unclear whether he was able to understand what he was looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll ask him. Although studying in Oxford without knowledge of the English language might not be that easy. You read and speak English, Mr. Kovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. However, I would prefer to testify in my own language, in Serbian, and to have questions put to me to the extent possible in that same language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the problem. The problem is that there -- have you reviewed your CV which is exclusively available in the English language? Have you reviewed it on its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think I already pronounced it was admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it was admitted but we don't have the number because there was so many speakers at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1367 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And at this point in time I would urge Mr. Stojanovic and the witness to pause between question and answer. Otherwise, it's not possible to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kovic, tell us, what was the specific task you were given by the Defence of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: I was given the task of studying four documents, these are actually reports of two experts, Robert Donia and Patrick Treanor. Two reports by Robert Donia: The background, policy and strategy of the siege of Sarajevo from 1991 until 1995, and also relevant excerpts from debates in the Assembly of Republika Srpska from 1992 until 1995. As I've already said, these are two reports. There are, rather, two reports by Patrick Treanor: The leadership of the Bosnian Serbs from 1990 until 1992 -- excuse me, and the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs from 1993 until 1995. My task was to give my own assessment regarding the academic and factual reliability of these documents. That is to say, as a historian, to do everything that a historian is trained to do. Anybody involved in the humanities. That is to say, to write a review of these four documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, the last things you said, that they appear in your report as well, There is no need to repeat what is already in the report because that's in the introductory paragraphs, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, as for your paper and your task, did you actually compile several reports?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I submitted two reports to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, I would like us to go through your report briefly, the one that you entitled: Analysis of a report entitled: The Bosnian Serb leadership, 1990 to 1992, and the Bosnian Serb leadership from 1993 until 1995 by expert Professor Patrick Treanor and the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 1D05904 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is this the front page of one of these reports of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please briefly just go through some of the main highlights of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in B/C/S, could we have page 3, and in English, page 3, the second paragraph from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, here, you dealt with the phrase "Bosnian Serbs" and then you elaborated on that; namely, why you consider this phrase, "Bosnian Serbs," to be incorrect professionally and historically. Please do not repeat everything that is contained in your report, but I would just like to ask you to briefly tell the Court about the key points underlying this assessment; namely that this phrase should not be included in the Prosecution expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: It is imprecise. And it's even incorrect. It is imprecise because all Serbs who were in the leadership of Republika Srpska that are referred to these reports were not Bosnians. Some of them were from Herzegovina. It would be the same thing like telling a person from Utrecht that he is from The Hague. I don't know what else to say. For example, Radovan Karadzic is from Herzegovina. Let me not repeat everything that I've written. Telling him that is he a Bosnian, well, I don't know how a person from Herzegovina would react that. So it is imprecise. Politically it is controversial because to tell somebody who lives in Republika Srpska today that is he a Bosnian Serb, he would take offence. He is a Serb from Republika Srpska. Somehow one would expect a greater degree of caution, academic, methodological, and also a bit more human fairness from someone who is supposed to be a serious author of this kind of text. It is also a political issue because one of the reasons for the war was certainly the rejection of the Serbs who live in Bosnia-Herzegovina to be declared Bosnian Serbs. It was a major political issue even in the socialist Yugoslavia; namely, the literature from Sarajevo, would it be called the literature of Bosnia-Herzegovina or literature from Bosnia-Herzegovina? One of the greatest Muslim authors from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mesa Selimovic, refused to be an author of Bosnia-Herzegovinian literature. If you understand what I'm saying. It's a question of dissatisfaction on the part of this Muslim writer. And many Serbs, they viewed this as an attempt to be assimilated into something that would be a Bosnian political entity or a Bosnian nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 7, B/C/S, and page 6, third paragraph of the report in English - your report, Professor - as you criticise Mr. Treanor's paper you say, inter alia, that such research would have to contain the sources of the other conflicting sides as well. In historiography, each subject requires to be viewed from various angles which allows for more nuanced conclusions especially when dealing with wars and international crises. That is what you call the reason for saying that these reports are one-sided. My question: Is this a scientific approach by Mr. Treanor, and would the conclusions based on such a methodological approach be scientific and scholarly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: What I wrote was that this should not be the approach of a historian. Quite simply, as far as wars are concerned, and here we do have a civil war that is being dealt with, you cannot view the phenomenon properly if you don't view it from different angles. Professor Treanor used intercepts between Radovan Karadzic and his associates. That is of interest and that is an interesting source, but then a reader wonders where are the intercepted conversations of Alija Izetbegovic and Ejup Ganic or, for example, Ejub Ganic and Abu Hamza Al-Masri, one of the Mujahedin there. He is in Guantanamo Bay nowadays. So can one imagine what would be contained there. This is basic. This is something that is taught during one's freshman year at university. Audiatur et altera pars. So dealing with the Bosnian Serbs, that is fine, but he goes into political assessments. He is judging the participants. In order to do that, you really have to be very cautious and you have to study different sources from different sides very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at page 9 of your report in B/C/S and page 7, the last sentence in the fourth paragraph, where you say, among other things -- again, speaking of the question of bias in the report by

utterances.speaker: MR. TREANOR
utterances.text: "The author views the Serbian secession within Bosnia-Herzegovina as something separate from what was happening in Yugoslavia. As we will see, he does not attach any special importance even to the secessionism of Bosnian Muslims and Croats from Yugoslavia." Professor, tell us briefly, please, why you believe that such a conclusion requires necessarily a broader context of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: There are three methodological objections. First, one-sided sources. Second, bias, the bias that is obvious in the language used. Analyse this discourse and you will see it. And, three, he is taking facts out of their historical context. The author, Patrick Treanor, wrote in his introduction that his main purpose is to represent the real historical context of what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990 to 1995. His two reports. That's precisely the problem. You cannot understand the Serbian secession within Bosnia-Herzegovina unless you understand the secession of Muslims and Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Croats from Yugoslavia. It's a far more complex problem than I can say in a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not now, Professor, thank you, because our time is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us stay on the same page in B/C/S. And, in the English version could we see page 8, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, Professor, you say that the key moves of the Serbs in the period from 1990 through 1995, and especially in 1992, 1992 -- in 1990 to 1992, were actually compelled, forced by the moves of the Muslims and Croats. Why do you believe so?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: In all secessionist wars, the one who secedes takes the lead. Remember Belgium. That's the case almost everywhere in history where secessionism is involved. The first actions were taken by Muslims and Croats who wanted independence or, as Alija Izetbegovic put it, sovereignty even at the price of peace; whereas the Serbs only wanted the status quo to remain, to remain in Yugoslavia. So all the moves of the Serbs were forced moves. Of course, during the war, one or the other side would occasionally take the offensive, but the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started as a secessionist war in which the Serbs were trying to respond to the moves of the secessionists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you now how does the report of Mr. Treanor view the theories that are you presenting today in the courtroom concerning forced secessionism?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: The problem is that the author forgets the context and thus the actions of the Serb appear in a sort of vacuum. We don't see what's going on around them. Every political move is an answer to something. But when you exclude the context as the report of Mr. Treanor did, you could say that France attacked Germany in 1914. You know that Germany was preparing for war. You know how Britain was watching Hitler's Germany before the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, we're still on the same subject. Let us look at page 13 of your report in B/C/S and page 10, the last paragraph, in English. Among other things, you say, elaborating on this subject: "... the planned Slovene, Croat, and Muslim breaking up of Yugoslavia but the unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be defended at all costs." Is there a reasoning behind this description?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The problem in all these papers that I analysed is inconsistency. Everyone has to defend their country, but not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the -- could the -- could the witness please start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you repeat your answer on from the beginning. And could you slow down in speaking. So you were asked whether there's a reasoning behind this description. You said: Of course. And could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear that the secessionisms of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia as well as the secessionisms of Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina are interlinked. This is again another phenomenon which is the logical inconsistency of the author. If you are for a multi-ethnic society - and you are, and in my view it's a reasonable position - how can you then support secessionist breaking up of a multi-ethnic Yugoslavia which was a federal state, a federal country, while at the same time supporting the preservations at all costs of a multinational unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina. In my view, it is illogical. Moreover, in the report by Robert Donia, supporting also unitarian Croatia because the right of Serbian Krajina to exist is disputed. So you are breaking up the multi-ethnic Yugoslavia while wanting to preserve a unitarian multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina. In my view, that is illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that it is, indeed, illogical, what you've just described --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, whether it is illogical or not, the witness has told us. It is not for you to say that he is right in telling us that. Yes? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to sum up, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What you have just told us, would it be scientifically also unjustified to draw the conclusions Mr. Treanor drew?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Science requires consistency in work, so in that sense this is inconsistent. I would just like to say that Professor John Fine, who is a friend and associate and mentor of Professor Robert Donia, John Fine who published a book together with Donia on Bosnia-Herzegovina, insists on the illogical points that I underlined. John Fine says that if you are for the preservation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then it would be logical for you to also support the preservation of Yugoslavia. The principle of multi-nationalism and multi-culturality is at stake. Yugoslavia was really the whole world -- Europe in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The name you said, John Fine. How is -- could you spell the name Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. [In English] F-i-n-e. [Interpretation] That's his last name, F-i-n-e. John Fine. He is a senior colleague and mentor of Robert Donia, like Milorad Ekmecic was in Sarajevo with whom Professor Donia collaborated also. But John Fine collaborated with Donia more closely and published a book together with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could we now look at page 14 in B/C/S; and, in English, that would be page 11, paragraph 3, where you say, among other things: "As Robert Hayden says, the criteria that the Badinter Commission applied to Yugoslavia when it concluded that it was in the process of disintegration could logically and consistently have been applied to Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. These criteria meant simple encouragement for any separatist movement which would be able to declare independence and withdraw from the central organs of government." My first question is: Could you tell us in more detail, in a few sentences, who is Robert Hayden? And my second question: If, according to the Badinter Commission, the SFRY was disintegrating, could Bosnia-Herzegovina also under the same criteria be treated as a country in the process of disintegration from your professional scientific point of view?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Robert Hayden is a professor at the University of Pittsburgh and he teaches law, international relations and anthropology, so at the University of Pittsburgh. And he is well known for his field research in Yugoslavia and in India. I invoked the results that he obtained, and he says that the criteria under which a state is in the process of disintegration when it does not have control over its entire territory and when all its parts are not represented in joint institutions, that principle could have applied to Yugoslavia at the time of its dissolution but also to Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992. That is his conclusion and I believe it is rather convincing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Treanor deal with this issue in his report at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us while we stay on the same page in B/C/S and move to page -- in fact, move to the last sentence on this page in English and then turn the page as we are reading. So page 12, the first sentence: "In the opinion of Steven Burg and Paul Shoup, Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised prematurely under pressure from the USA. According to them, independence should have been made conditional on an agreement between the three sides on the constitutional order." First of all, would you tell us who these two authors are, and then tell us your views on the premature recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as Mr. Treanor's treatment of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: In one of the footnotes, Robert Donia recognises Steven Burg and Paul Shoup as the most senior researchers of this issue. These are people who did not start in this area yesterday. Professor Paul Shoup is professor emeritus at the University of Virginia. He has many publications that are not linked to these issues, such as Eastern Europe, et cetera. Steven Burg teaches at a smaller university near Boston. I'll remember the name of the university later. I am inclined to agree with their conclusions. Instead of organising the negotiations between the three parties to reach whatever agreement could be reached, recognition was declared instead. That's also the view of Lord Carrington and these two authors are not the only people who say the same things. They say that in the case of Croatia as in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the sides should have been forced to negotiate first. Instead, both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were recognised prematurely and then what happened happened. I'm trying to say that major powers, major countries, often make very serious mistakes in their foreign policy and these mistakes are paid by the citizens of the countries that make such mistakes as well as the citizens of the countries that are the subject of such decisions. That is my opinion. And the participants of these events are listed on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to page 16 in B/C/S, and page 13, paragraph 1, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, as you analysed all these theses of Professor Treanor, you present, inter alia, another interesting theory where you say Alija Izetbegovic also rejected the so-called Belgrade initiative, an agreement reached with Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic in July 1991. On the other side was Adil Zulfikarpasic, one of the founders of the SDA, and his associates from the Muslim Bosniak association. My question, my question: Do you think that an objective analyst, a historian, should deal with the failure of this initiative in his report as well and the consequences that followed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Belgrade initiative from July 1991 is not mentioned in Professor Treanor's reports and it's not mentioned in Professor Donia's reports. So this is yet another objection. That is to say, having certain facts omitted. We haven't referred to that yet. So one of the founders of the SDA, Adil Zulfikarpasic, Muhamed Filipovic also, and their associates, in July 1991, reached agreement first with the Serbs from Republika Srpska, then Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then with Slobodan Milosevic. It had to do with the preservation of Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia would have been organised as a federal state and Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been organised as a unitary federal unit. Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina were prepared to give up on everything they had attained so far in terms of the decentralisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Adil Zulfikarpasic wrote a lot about that, and he showed that Alija Izetbegovic until the very last moment supported the initiative and then abruptly he abandoned the entire idea and Adil Zulfikarpasic himself. Why is this idea important? It shows that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were prepared to live in a joint multi-ethnic Yugoslav state. Everything that happened later were forced moves due to the secession of the Bosnian Muslims and Croats. At the same time, it shows that the Muslim leadership was not united. Adil Zulfikarpasic, who lived in Switzerland for a long time in the west and he represented a more liberal wing, and I would say that the difference between him and Alija Zulfikarpasic [as interpreted] is that Alija Zulfikarpasic is an Islamist whereas Zulfikarpasic is a nationalist. So that is something that happened between the Bosnian Muslims themselves. Zulfikarpasic was in favour of something else and also the -- the position of the president of that state was offered to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Alija Izetbegovic and -- So Alija Izetbegovic was offered the position of president of that state and he refused that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask for clarification. Can I ask for clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovic, at page 16, line 8, you are recorded as having said Yugoslavia would have been organised as a federal state, and Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been organised as a unitary federal unit. I'm not quite sure I understand what a unitary federal unit is. Are you -- if that's how you expressed it, can you give us an explanation. Or if you were misquoted, can you give us the correct quote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I said here was that Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain within the Yugoslav Federation. That is to say, Yugoslavia would be a federal state. It would consist of Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, it would be a federal state. However, Bosnia-Herzegovina itself would not be federalised as such. Bosnia-Herzegovina would be one of the federal units. It would be centralised in terms of its organisation. It would not have any separate entities and so on. So Bosnia itself would be based on a unitary principle. That is what Adil Zulfikarpasic asked for. He said that that was the red line and he didn't want to go beyond that in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. Herzegovina, is that exclusively Serb populated? Or are there living Croats and Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Of course. The Neretva River flows through Herzegovina. It is multi-ethnic by definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you've answered that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have to go into details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Page 16, line 17 and 18, you were talking about what the Bosnian Muslims and Croats did. Now, would the Herzegovinian Muslims and Croats be offended by the use of that language of yours? Because you criticised Mr. Treanor that much about talking about Bosnian Serbs because they could be from Herzegovina. You are using the term "Bosnian Muslim and Croats," would they be -- would they feel similarly offended by your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly, I don't think so, because there is something that is called the Bosniak idea. The Muslims do not insist on these differences. If you wish, I can deal with this in detail. The Bosnian nation that was created by Benjamin Kallay in the 19th century, the Austro-Hungarian authorities, there's this Bosniak and Bosnian idea. Of course, Bosnian Muslims have their own view, but they would not be offended the same way the Serbs would be offended in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the Croats? Do they have a similar position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as Croats are concerned, there would be nuances involved. The majority of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina live in Herzegovina. Although there are some in Bosnia. They emphasize this kind of difference more. So this Bosnian idea, one can say that Croats did not accept it. Just like Serbs did not want to accept it. I can elaborate on this, if you wish. All of these questions have a historical dimension -- yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you explained your criticism by referring to people from -- I think from Utrecht would be offended if they would be said to be from another town. You didn't give any nuance, you just said because they were born elsewhere. Therefore I do understand now that there's a lot of nuance in that and that it's not just a matter of inaccuracy by a historian but that there is far more involved. And if I understand you well, you are including a lot of things you have not raised in your report in this respect about how offensive it would be or would not be. Is that -- would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I understand. I think that I understand what you tried to say. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that. However, may I just say one thing? I think that one should make a distinction between what is written as an expert report and what is sometimes stated in the course of a conversation. We always try not to offend anyone. But when we write a document that is supposed to be admitted into evidence, here we have to exercise additional caution. That is the only thing I wished to say in addition to what I've already said, and I think I understand the point that you made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And such nuances on which you insist now are missing in the portion where you say how offensive Mr. Treanor's language is. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that I understood your question or perhaps it's a question of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's offensive to call someone from Utrecht as if he was born elsewhere, without any further nuances whether some people from Utrecht might feel, others might not. All those nuances are not in your written report where you criticise Mr. Treanor, or did I miss it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I made an effort to take these nuances into account. It is one thing where you make a mistake when you're speaking and if you perhaps tell someone who is from Utrecht that he is from The Hague and vice versa. However, if the person from Utrecht is on trial, and if you are writing something that is supposed to be evidence against that person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. There's no evidence against a person here. There's evidence to give the Court the opinion of an expert. At least we do not expect you to testify in favour of Mr. Mladic nor against Mr. Mladic. We expect you to give your expert opinion in full independence and in accordance with your profession. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I've said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as far as the papers of Patrick Treanor are concerned -- oh, I see. Oh, we should continue. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just one more question related to your first report. Thank you for the effort you have made. Could we please take a look at page 21 in B/C/S and in the English version of your report it is page 16, the last sentence. It then continues on page 17. This is what you say: "Finally, the context cannot be even the confidently pronounced value judgements and criticisms of only one side in a civil war. All in all, this lack of context caused the authors writing about the basic subject to seem unhistorical, completely void of cause and consequence or a realistic temporal and spatial framework." However, this is what my question is. You used a phrase here and said that it was a civil war. Please tell us as briefly as possible why you qualified the developments of Bosnia-Herzegovina in such a way, as a civil war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not the only one to qualify what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina in this way. This phrase is customary in science and it is a subject of debate. However, in my view, this is yet another sad, terrible war that has afflicted the population of our lands for centuries. It is basically the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are wars in which neighbours are at war, neighbours who speak the same language. Now we call that language our language. It used to be called Serbo-Croat before. These are people who have different religions. And this is a terrible fate of the Bosnian peoples, but they are not the only ones responsible for that. Unfortunately, someone from outside wishes to encourage such conflicts. For example, like in 16th-century France or 17th-century Germany. It's that kind of civil war. Can you call them religious wars too. However, someone who is a believer cannot destroy a place of worship of any religion. So it is a question of whether these are religious wars or not. However, the war went along religious lines like in the 16th century, like in the 17th century, like during the genocide against the Serbs by the independent state of Croatia in the Second World War. People being reduced to their religious affiliations and not paying attention to what their joint interests are, their common fate, their neighbourly relations. That's why I'm saying this is a civil war. It had some other factors involved as well, but essentially, that is a repetition of what happened there in 1941, 1945, of course, in a different historical context, and then 1914 and 1918, and not to go into the 19th century. In Europe, these wars ended when the Thirty Years' War ended and also after the Treaty of Versailles. In Europe, wars do not have this dimension. However, in the Balkans this continued because of the wars between Austro-Hungary, Turkey, not to go into too much detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, professor. Now that you took the solemn declaration in this courtroom, now that we went through your report, today, do you fully stand by your written report that you entitled: The leadership of the Bosnian Serbs 1990-1992, and the analysis of Mr. Treanor's report for 1992 and 1993-1995? Is that your fully accepted report in this courtroom today as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after the cross-examination, I would like to tender 1D05904 into evidence. That is Professor Kovic's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually the decision is taken at the end of the testimony of the witness, so may I take it that you want it to be marked for identification? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D1368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1368 is marked for identification. It's time for the break, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. After the break, we're going to go through the other report, and I think that I will stay within my time-limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Kovic. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you also make a report for the Defence of General Mladic which you titled: Analysis of the expert report by Robert Donia on the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the case Prosecutor against Ratko Mladic, and submit that report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court, please, 65 ter 1D05905.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is this the cover page of your report? You have it before you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now display in e-court page 6 in B/C/S. And in English that would be page 5, second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, along the same principles we followed when discussing your previous report and without repeating what is elaborated in detail in your report, could you please highlight the main points that I ask you about. Here, you say, I quote: "The term 'siege' is contentious because the besieged maintained links with the outside world through the UN peacekeeping forces ..." And you go on to explain how and in which ways. And in the next paragraph, which is on page 7 in B/C/S, you say: "Sarajevo between 1992 and 1995 was a divided but not a besieged city." My question is: Professor, why do you believe the term used by Professor Donia, namely, the "siege of Sarajevo," is incorrect and that the term "divided city" would be more appropriate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't this clearly explained in the report? I mean, unless you'd like to add something to it, but then ask specifically on what. But I think it's clearly explained in the report, isn't it? East Sarajevo, west Sarajevo, well, it's all clearly explained, so why ask again what we have read already? So if you have any focussed question, please proceed, but don't ask the witness to repeat what he has written down already in some detail. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I've already said that I would not like to hear anything from the report repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But in view of what we discussed in the preparations for your appearance in court, could you just tell us why, from the historical point of view, the term "divided" is more appropriate than the term "besieged."

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: In my view, there are two concepts that could be used. One is used by Robert Donia in his second report, the struggle for Sarajevo. And the second concept is a divided city. What I did not write in my report and what I would like to say now is this. If you take the centre of The Hague and proclaim it to be The Hague and you say that Scheveningen is not The Hague, and if, God forbid, Scheveningen gets into conflict with the centre of The Hague, and then if you have proclaimed the centre of The Hague to be The Hague, then could you call it the siege of The Hague. But if you treat these two parts as two districts then, it would be a divided city. Of course, this is a clearly hypothetical situation. Also, and I didn't write this in my report, General Michael Rose in his memoirs of his service in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994 says that his opinion was that Sarajevo was not a besieged city because it maintained links with the outside world thanks to the United Nations, and thanks to a series of other details that can be further discussed. In Sarajevo, you have, on the one hand, Serb forces; and on the other hand, you have those whom Professor Donia calls defenders. And in his monograph on Sarajevo, he says himself that 90 per cent of them were of Muslim ethnicity, which means that you have two armies in conflict that belonged to two different ethnic groups. That's the point of view from which I treated the term "siege of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 9 in B/C/S and page 7 in English, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, briefly, Professor, when you talk about the contexts of the reports made by Mr. Donia, you say again what is missing is the previous history of the war in Sarajevo. Is that a general academic objection to the -- to the approach taken by Professor Donia when writing his report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Professor Donia himself says in his introduction that he would be describing the context, and my main objection is precisely the lack of context. Not only was insufficient attention paid to the actions of the leaderships of the Croats and Muslims, and, if you wish, the US and NATO because they were also parties to that conflict until 1995, there is also a lack of serious attention to the context of the civil war. I have a correction to make to the interpretation. They are parties to that conflict from 1995, not until 1995. There is no clear context that would encompass the war in Croatia because the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina were involved in that war. It's clear that somebody from Croatia would wish to cause a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, in my opinion. And what is lacking is a longer historical introduction to what happened during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That would include at least the history of the NDH, the independent state of Croatia, from World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were making a correction to the translation. That's what we usually do not -- if you think that there's a problem, you can tell us and then it will be verified. But it's not for you to correct our translators. If you have some concerns in that respect, you may raise that, and then it will be reviewed on the basis of the audio, so we'll then know what you said how it was translated. But it is not for you to correct them. Yes? But if there's any concern, please do not hesitate to bring it to our attention. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at page 12 of your report in B/C/S, and page 9, the middle of the second paragraph, where you express a methodological objection to the report of Professor Donia, saying: "That is why it is surprising that the author of this report uses Muslim press reports from the war in Sarajevo and taking headlines from Muslim newspapers as a source of information about the war without comparing and cross-referencing these reports with those carried by, for example, the Serbian or Croatian press." Very briefly, Professor, in scientific practice and in historical analysis, what is the scope, the potential and the quality of sources such as newspapers of one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: For historians, press reports are a precious source, a valuable source to establish what happened, but they are much more important as a source of information about editorial policy and the political position of a given newspaper. In that sense, historians are very cautious in determining facts and events based on the press. The press is primarily a source of the political position of a newspaper or a television studio. When you have a war in which several parties are involved and you see a headline from a newspaper Chetniks -- Sarajevo is targeted by Chetniks, or in -- is in the cross-hairs of the Chetniks, "Chetniks" being a very pejorative term, then it is very important to compare it to the Serbian and Croatian press. Wherever you have a war, you have war propaganda. That's why using such sources is methodologically very questionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the same page in the second paragraph from the bottom in English you say, continuing to elaborate these objections to the report by Professor Donia: "The author also establishes the course of events in the former Yugoslavia on the basis of published analyses and reports of the American Central Intelligence Agency ... and elsewhere without comparing them with data from other sources." Why do you want to emphasise this particular objection in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: To this day, we continue to use materials from the CIA, but we all know what the CIA is. Quite simply, it is necessary to show methodological caution when using sources of such provenance. Of course, we can use them. There are publications that are very valuable and important among them, but there is a lack of sufficient caution here. The CIA, the US, and NATO got involved in this conflict, and they were a party to the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following question. Have you considered -- because we're interested in what you're telling us. In cross-referencing where Mr. Donia uses reports which you say are one-sided, have you tried -- have you verified whether other sources deal with the same matter and have you considered to bring that to our attention? Because saying that Mr. Donia is wrong is one thing, but to give us the full picture by making that cross-reference and say, Well, what you consider to be propaganda on the one side, there's other information. Have you considered to do that so that we would have a more complete picture of what you say Mr. Donia is describing in a one-sided way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have done that. Precisely in this report. Specific examples are battles in the centre of Sarajevo in 1992. The author described it only on one page, and I provided other sources. And the fighting -- the massacre in Pofalici. There also I provided Serbian sources where I called it a massacre of civilians more cautiously. So comparing sources, if I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I've seen examples. But have you systematically done the same so as to give us the full picture on the whole of the report of Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My task was to review this report. Had I tried to create a comprehensive picture as to how events should be interpreted, that would have constituted a separate monograph. So in my report, I gave proof concerning matters that are not contained in the report. Therefore, the picture that I am portraying has to be a fragmentary one by definition. I did not attempt to provide a comprehensive picture of what happened. I am reviewing, criticizing, Professor Donia and Professor Treanor, so this mosaic which is incomplete, I am adding some tiles that would provide a more comprehensive picture in terms of what had happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that in the context of the task that was given to you by the Defence. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, now let us move on to page 23 in B/C/S of your report. And it's page 17, the second paragraph from the bottom, in English. As you analyse Professor Donia's reports in his chapter 2 that is entitled: The transformation of the JNA, you say: "The actions of the JNA were forced. Rather, the JNA was therefore forced to act, and this can be said not only of its actions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also the actions of the VRS. It was the secessionists who set events in motion in Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina." Professor, just briefly, in your view, how is this forced hand shown?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: As far as Sarajevo is concerned, if your barracks are encircled and if they're opening fire at you - and that is, indeed, what happened in Sarajevo - then, of course, they force your hand. So General Kukanjac was seeking a response to something that was a specific challenge. That goes for Croatia as well. So when Robert Donia is writing about JNA attacks against Sarajevo, then it is only proper for him to say that barracks are under siege. Barracks and facilities of the JNA. So you're being attacked. What else can you do? You can either defend yourself or can you surrender. In this report, for example, there is not a single word about the garrison in Varazdin that surrendered and the one in Virovitica, but there are many that defended themselves, that did not surrender. And then there are other matters that we discussed. Of course, I can provide arguments for this later, if necessary. Secessionists were more active, especially if they get support from elsewhere. Then that is the basic precondition for the success of secession. So that was the struggle waged by the American colonies, then the Belgian independence, and, if you will, the former Yugoslavia as the lands were freeing themselves from Ottoman rule. But that is a separate question altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us please elaborate on this part of your sentence, where you are saying that it's also the actions of the VRS that were forced.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: It is true that Robert Donia referred to that in his report as well; namely, that party-based armies were being set up, the SDA, the HDZ, that they were working on establishing armed units. However, he provides that information ten pages after he had -- presenting incriminating views of Radovan Karadzic, so he is taking things out of context. Chronology and context are very important in this respect. There's a great deal of information involved - I imagine that I don't have had to go into detail now - starting May 1990, when they refused to surrender the weapons of the Territorial Defence, the -- that is something that Donia refers to then. The first steps taken to establish armed forces of the SDA. And so on and so forth. I don't want to go into detail now. Then what happened in western Herzegovina where the Army of the neighbouring republic of Croatia came in. So you have the presentation of Croatian armed forces in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is seemingly not one of the topics dealt with in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: However, what is a key question, speaking of the point of view of the tasks that were given to you, is as follows: An objective historian writing such a report, would he have to taken into account that context as well when drawing his conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. That's why I said that in this way you can prove anything. That France attacked Germany in 1914, for instance. Or that Israel and only Israel is responsible for the 1967 war. So you have to look at sources and actions of both sides not only one, and you cannot take the actions of the other side out of context even when you do mention them, and that is very rare here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness, please. Can I take you back to the war in the former Yugoslavia. You were asked by Mr. Stojanovic, you should elaborate on this part of your sentence where you are saying that it's also the actions of the VRS that were forced. You gave a very long answer but I didn't hear anything about how the VRS was forced into action. Can you explain that briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very gladly. The VRS was established in May 1992. It's the 12th of May that is referred to. At that moment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a -- already a war that was under way. That is to say, barracks were being attacked as Donia himself says. In the beginning of 1992 there were conflicts already. However, it was the worst in April and in May. I provided that conversation between General Adzic and Alija Izetbegovic. Artillery attacks, mortar attacks at the centre of the 2nd Military District on the 2nd of May in Sarajevo. Then also it is well-known that in the month of April the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, these are party armies of the SDA, they grow into the Territorial Defence and later on this is going to become the Army of the BH. I repeat, regular troops of the Republic of Croatia enter the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sijekovac, near Bosanski Brod, in May 1992. Serb civilians were slaughtered and all of that preceded the establishment of the VRS. So what were the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina supposed to do then? There's another thing that I did not mention. Then there is the creation of the Croat party army as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, a very long answer, but you are not really focussing on what you have written in your report. "Actions of the VRS were forced." Not the -- the foundation of the VRS, according to your report, but actions of the VRS. Which kinds of actions and how were they forced? This was the question of Mr. Stojanovic. You really should focus on questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that I quite understand your question. I spoke about the moment when the VRS was established. That is to say, their hand was forced there. If you're asking me about the actions that followed, on the one hand, you have secessionists that are referred to in this sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you again. I'm referring to it the paragraph we see on the screen: "The JNA was therefore forced to act ... but also the actions the VRS ..." What does that mean? It stands alone and I don't know the context, and Mr. Stojanovic asked you to elaborate about this short sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very brief answer. This is the Army of Republika Srpska. There is a war going on. There are adversary armies that are armed. You have two possibilities. You can either surrender or defend yourself. The creation of party-based armies of the Muslims and Croats preceded the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska. In my view, that is an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'll go back to that part that you mentioned, the part of Professor Donia's report. And in that context, can we look at page 79 in B/C/S, your report. It is page 58, the third paragraph from the bottom in the English version. You give an example here of Professor Donia mentioning the suffering of the Serbs in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, and you quote a sentence of his: "The lot of those Serbs had also become one of the most controversial aspects of the siege." And then you say: "Of course, when they declared that the civil, ethnic war in Sarajevo was a battle between good and evil, the persecution of Serbs had to become controversial ..." Question -- my question: Methodologically speaking, as you were objecting to Professor Donia, why did you find it necessary to accentuate this; namely, that when he mentions the fate of the Serbs in Sarajevo, he says that that is the most controversial aspect of the siege, one of the most controversial aspects of the siege?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: This was taken from Donia's book, Sarajevo. It's actually not even contained in the report that was submitted to this Court. This sentence is not there either. So I said that in his monograph, the author does have that one single sentence where he refers to Serb victims in Sarajevo. And then there is this sentence about the battle of Pofalici, which is again from his book, Sarajevo. It's not from his report. In my view, to put it very mildly, it is very controversial, to say the least, to write about the war in Sarajevo without any reference to Serb victims, and that is exactly was done in this report. It is shocking. This is a quotation from the author's book and it is controversial. Let me not repeat what I wrote here, but if we take as a point of departure that the war in Sarajevo is a war between good and evil, and that the Serbs are evil and the others are the good ones, then perhaps that is part of the answer to His Honour's question. Then you have what happened in Pofalici and then the VRS took action. I don't need to repeat this. In Pofalici, there was a showdown with Serb nationalists. That's what Donia says in his book. You should at least mention the civilian victims in Pofalici. What do Serb sources say about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your explanation. Are you referring to a book published by Mr. Donia or his report provided to the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These quotations, these two sentences that were read out are from the book. It's a monograph entitled: Sarajevo, written by Robert Donia. And it's only there that he mentions the fate of these Serbs. In the report that was submitted to the Court here, there is no mention of that. The private prisons for Serbs. No mention of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now take a look at page 83 in B/C/S - the B/C/S version of your report, Professor - and that is page 61, second paragraph. Underneath the heading, you quote Michael Rose, the commander of UNPROFOR, where he said: "By mid-1994, the Bosnian government undoubtedly stopped supporting the UN peace efforts, believing that a cease-fire could turn into a permanent freeze of the lines of conflict, which would then result in an unfair division of the country." Let me not read on. I will end with the following sentence: "The Bosnian army had an additional goal, to draw the UN and NATO into a land war." Since this is a quotation from Mr. Rose's book, this is what I have to ask you: As you studied developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically in Sarajevo, did you find that these conclusions of Mr. Rose were right, or, as an objective historian, could one come to a different conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: General Michael Rose is not the only one to have presented such a view. In his memoirs, he keeps repeating it. He is very critical of the Serb side as well. However, he is also convinced that in 1994, the Presidency - Alija Izetbegovic and his associates - were trying to make the US and NATO intervene. And bearing that goal in mind, they are prepared to expose their own citizens to suffering. In the Islamic Declaration of Alija Izetbegovic, which was reprinted in 1990, there is that horrifying sentence that says a people who are asleep have to be awakened with blows, and he is heralding an era of suffering for his own people. That is almost verbatim what he says. I quoted it in my report. It is horrifying and, of course, it is up to the historians of Sarajevo, among others, to show what it was that happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, finally, I would like to us look at page 87 of the B/C/S version of your report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we do that, I have one question with respect to the footnote 165 -- no, sorry, I mixed up two matters. I withdraw, and please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I would have a question. You said, Witness, that General Rose was also very critical about the Serbs. Where is that exactly to be found in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what? In the report that I analysed, there is ample criticism of the Serbian side and you will find quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My task, my assignment was to critique the text of Robert Donia and Patrick Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You apparently are explaining something. Do I have to understand that you have not dealt with that for the reasons you start explaining without telling us that you haven't dealt with the critical remarks by General Rose in relation to the Serbs? You explained why you left that out. Is that -- or why you didn't think it -- that you needed -- yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the simple answer is: I didn't deal with it. And then you can give the reasons or Mr. Stojanovic will ask for the reasons and that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I did not include it. And the reason is that this report on 120 pages ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will go back to page 87 in B/C/S, and page 64, paragraph 3 from the bottom, in the English version of your report. There, Professor, you say: "However, Robert Donia does not mention the Zimmermann-Izetbegovic episode. On the contrary, he briefly announces, in only one sentence, that the Cutileiro Plan was rejected by all three sides. When discussing the discussion on responsibility, one would expect that this controversial element of the role and responsibility of the USA would at least be mentioned." My question is: Is there any historical information about the position of the US that the BH should not accept the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. And I expected the author to mention at least some basic things about it. You have references to the writing of David Binder, a major figure in American journalism, where Zimmermann describes his discussions with Alija Izetbegovic. And he says that Alija Izetbegovic is unhappy with the agreement and Zimmermann's answer is: Why did you sign it then? It was published in the "New York Times" and there is an exact reference. However, in his memoirs later, Zimmermann toned down his role in this discussion. Donia refers to David Binder and he says today, meaning 1993, when Binder published this -- who says, I think we were wrong when we convinced Izetbegovic to reject it. So this discussion about the Cutileiro Plan could be very different. From an objective historian, we would at least expect that he explain to us what really happened there. You have to present the basic things. All the time this basic issue arises of history as a profession and the work of the court where we, both of us, are trying to establish what really happened. But we see that the ability of a historian to help, to be of assistance is rather limited. I suppose that Mr. Donia did his best.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of this answer, do you as a historian believe that in a report such as the one authored by Mr. Donia, there should also be a discussion of the consequences of rejecting the Cutileiro Plan on the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the country as such?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: I would even say that this kind of normative issue does not have to be posed by a historian. The question of good fortune or bad fortune depends also on the ideology of the historian. But in his two reports, he actually presented some value judgements, his own positions, his political positions, and that's why it be would a good thing if he had posed that question. What did the rejection of the Cutileiro Plan bring to the Croats, Muslims, and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Considering that later in Dayton Bosnia-Herzegovina was divided into entities after all. This reminds us of the power of the major powers and their statesmen and the mistakes they make which are later paid by the regular citizens. And this is one of the major examples of a mistake made by the USA. I hope -- I believe it was not intentional, that it was an honest mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've made the solemn declaration in this courtroom, do you fully still stand by the report that you made for the needs of the Defence of General Mladic where you analysed the report of Robert Donia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my direct examination of Professor Kovic. And I should like this exhibit, 1D05905, to be MFI'd pending the completion of the cross-examination of Professor Kovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D1369, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Mr. Kovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You'll find Mr. Traldi to your right. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The two reports that we've discussed today are your first published works regarding events in the 1990s in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Depends on what you understand "published works" to mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's have Exhibit D1367.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is the CV you provided to the Defence and reviewed and was admitted into evidence earlier today. Turning to page 2, we see what are described as your principal publications. The first is a book: Disraeli and the Eastern Question. Now Disraeli is Benjamin Disraeli, a 19th-century British prime minister; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to one of these publications: Historiography in Serbia, developments since 1989. Now "historiography" is a term used for two ideas. First, the study of historian's methodology; and second, the body of historical scholarship on a particular subject. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: That's a question of terminology in the Serbian and English languages. When we say "historiography" in Serbian -- I don't want to go into too much detail. History is the science and history is also what happened. Historiography is a synonym for history as a science. That's how it was used here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Which means historiography since 1989 describes developments in the science of history; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: I think you are right. That is an overview of what Serbian historians published from 1989 onwards. It's a critical analysis. That's basically the same type of work that I did here. It's a critical analysis of text. I treat historical production as events that I analyse. That's similar to what I've done here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, is it right that your CV includes two articles about World War II and the remainder about events in even earlier periods of history?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. But I would say that in this CV you have four articles dedicated to Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 19th century. And if you have read my book about Disraeli, you will see that Bosnia-Herzegovina is in the focus of events and what I deal with is the treatment of major powers of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have to go back to the 19th century to understand what's happening today. You will not understand the policies of the Armenians if you don't understand the genocide against Armenians. The same applies to the situation of Israel, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I was desperately trying to find it on the present page. But you took us to page 4 of the CV where I find historiography --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have it on page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but not on page 2. If you would always take us to the page you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, it's right, then, now that we've gone through it, that these two reports are your first published works directly dealing with events that occurred in the 1990s in the former Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that. The war in Bosnia from 1992 through 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now before I get into the topics you discussed on direct examination, I have a couple of questions about other parts of your report. On page 51 of your Donia report, that is your report responding to expert Donia, you write: "The suffering of civilians of all ethnic groups in Sarajevo cannot be denied or justified." Would you agree that in your report and your testimony this morning you focus on the suffering of Serb civilians in Muslim-controlled Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And if you allow me to explain, I can tell you for what reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: -- that is missing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you've given that explanation on direct.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In what ways did you intend to convey in that sentence that Muslim civilians in the city of Sarajevo suffered during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: You have quite enough information about that in the report of Robert Donia that I analysed, which I reviewed. He avoids mentioning Serbian victims as if some victims had a value and others did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Should I take it, then, that you avoid mentioning Muslim victims because you do not challenge Dr. Donia's description of what happened to Muslim civilians inside the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: What I do challenge I mentioned in my report. I challenge it in many ways that we've already discussed, but I'm not challenging the suffering of Muslim civilians in Sarajevo or elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was not job. My job was to make a critical analysis of the text that I received. I have a lot of respect for everybody's suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you challenge that Muslim civilians inside the confrontation lines were terrorised by shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned terrorise. That's a term used in the indictment. And I believe that is wrong. And I explained why what happened in Sarajevo happened. The purpose was not to terrorise. The purpose was to maintain the military personnel of the Muslims, the armed force of the BH, and there was an obvious choice to divide the city. The purpose was not to terrorise. The victimisation was from indiscriminate shelling and sniping. But there was sniping also against Serbs who lived in Dobrinje, Nedzarici, Ilidza, and that is missing in Donia's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question for the gentleman. You say the purpose was not to terrorise. My question to you is: What was the effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like in all wars, people suffer, people are victimized. There was terror also against the Serbs. I repeat, I critiqued the texts that were handed to me. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not asking you about the critiquing the texts. I was just asking you what the effect was. You have told us there was terror, so the effect was terrorising. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you said a moment ago, as you say in your Donia report at page 62, that you believe the purpose was to maintain the military personnel of the Muslims, and you explain in the report, in a blockade. Now, if you blockade the urban core of a city, everyone in that urban core is stuck in there; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show me my report on my screen? I still see only my CV. It would be easier for me to follow your question. Let me go back, if I may, to the previous question. I did not claim that terror was the aim. The aim was to keep the enemy personnel. Even the issue of blockade is disputable. Look at the maps. All the maps showing combat positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina including Sarajevo, maps you can find on the Internet, you will see that Sarajevo is always connected to its hinterland. All maps that were not made in Banja Luka, you will see that Sarajevo is linked to its hinterland. It's not the same as Srebrenica and Zepa. It's an open blockade. Yes, the Serbs tried to block the eastern part and the Muslims were blocking Ilijas, Hadzici, et cetera. The Muslim part of Sarajevo goes into that Serb territory. If this Serbian part was also going into Muslim territory ending with Hadzici, we could also treat it as under blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P3. And I'll be looking for page 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, may I seek -- did I hear you well when you said: There was terror also against the Serbs. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are talking about terror against Muslims, then -- if we are using that term, then we should certainly be talking also about terror against the Serbs. That, in my opinion, would be logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not what you said. You said: "Like in all wars, people suffer, people are victimized. There was terror also against the Serbs." That's not: If you talk about terror against Muslims, then you should talk about terror against Serbs as well. You said: "There was also terror against Serbs." It -- we -- I heard you well, or at least I heard the translation well when you said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that question. In fact, you helped me clarify my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask to you do that. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the centre left part of this map. On the left circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is an SRK military map. We see red and blue lines. And we see in blue in what represents the urban part of Sarajevo 1K, and then we see the abbreviations for different SRK units ringing it. That urban part of Sarajevo is ringed by red lines for VRS forces; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC
